1. Determine which interval the given $ x $-value belongs to. 2. Use the corresponding equation to compute $ f(x) $.

cards.back: $ f(0) = 0-2 = -2 $ (use first piece). $ f(4) = 2(4)+1 = 9 $ (use second piece).

cards.back: Graph each piece only on its specified interval. Use [[imp:open circles]] for endpoints not included (<, >) and [[imp:closed circles]] for endpoints included (≤, ≥).
cards.front: How do you graph a piecewise function?
Graph $ y = \begin{cases} -x-4, & x<0 \\ x, & x\ge 0 \end{cases} $ and describe the domain and range.
cards.back: Left ray: open at (0,-4), slope -1. Right ray: closed at (0,0), slope 1. Domain: all real numbers. Range: $ y > -4 $.

cards.back: A piecewise function where each piece is a constant value. The graph looks like [[imp:stair steps]]. Often used for tiered pricing.

cards.front: A karaoke rental costs $50 for the first day and $25 per additional day. Write the step function for up to 3 days.

cards.back: Split at the point where the expression inside the absolute value is zero. For $ |x-h| $, if $ x-h < 0 $, use $ -(x-h) $; if $ x-h \ge 0 $, use $ x-h $. Then apply any multipliers and shifts.
cards.front: How do you write an absolute value function as a piecewise function?
Write $ y = |x-2| $ as a piecewise function.

cards.back: Split at $ x=-3 $. $ y = \begin{cases} -2x-6, & x<-3 \\ 2x+6, & x\ge -3 \end{cases} $
cards.front: Write $ y = 2|x+3| $ as a piecewise function.

cards.back: [[imp:Understand]]: identify pieces and their intervals. [[imp:Solve]]: find equation for each piece. [[imp:Conclude]]: write in piecewise notation with conditions.
Since $-2$ satisfies $-2\le x\le 5$, use the middle piece: $ f(-2) = -2+2 = 0 $.
cards.front: Evaluate $ f(x) = \begin{cases} 3, & x<-2 \\ x+2, & -2\le x\le 5 \\ 4x, & x>5 \end{cases} $ at $ x=-2 $.
Evaluate the same function at $ x=10 $.
cards.back: $ 10 > 5 $, so use the third piece: $ f(10) = 4(10) = 40 $.
The domain is the union of all intervals listed in the conditions. Each constant piece applies to a specific interval of $ x $.
